newsitem.title: UK: Mosvold confident of new pay off from old tankers.
newsitem.headline: Mosvold confident of new pay off from old tankers.

text.p: Mosvold Shipping ASA said it remains confident its recent expansion into 'vintage' tankers will succeed, despite reporting losses in the second quarter.
In June, the Norwegian tanker owner raised $32.7m through a rights issue to fund the acquisition and refurbishment of a further two ageing VLCCs, doubling the size of its large tanker fleet to four.
But initial costs of $1.6 million for the operation and repair of its two new vessels have dented results.
Magne Kristiansen, Mosvold president said: "We are convinced that our decision to go with these ships will pay off."
He added: "The quarter has been as we expected. The tanker charter market is very strong, which gives us confidence for the remainder of this year."
Mosvold earlier reported a second quarter pre-tax loss of $1.475 million against a pre-tax profit of $0.314 million in the same period a year earlier.
Costs associated with the acquisition of the two new vessels, Mosking and Mosqueen were $1.6 million, including $0.4m to cover damage to the boiler of the Mosking immediately after it was acquired.
Mosvold has gone against the current tanker industry consensus and invested in old tankers, rather than choosing to build new vessels.
Since the Exxon Valdez oil spill, shipping has faced regulatory pressure to replace old, single-hull tankers with new double-hulled vessels which are believed to be more environmentally safe.
Mosvold's rights issue prospectus said the firm aimed to: "Own large, vintage crude oil tankers of such a quality that they can be operated technically and commercially until they are 30 years old."

The Mosqueen and Mosking were built in 1974 and 1975 respectively by A.P. Moller's Lindo yard in Denmark for Shell, while the Moscliff and Mosocean were built in Germany n 1974 for Esso International.
When they reach 25 years of age, the vessels will face new international regulations that demand either structural alternations or impose loading restrictions.

"We face two alternatives: to load 'hydrostatically' so that in the event of an accident sea water will enter the tanks rather than oil leaking, or convert the tankers' side tanks to ballast tanks," said Kristiansen.
Hydrostatic loading would considerably reduce cargo capacity.

"We are already now converting some of the side tanks in both the Mosking and Mosqueen to ballast tanks. When completed they will be the first vessels in the world to have been adapted in this way for future operations," he added.
Mosking is currently in dry-dock in Dubai undergoing repairs.
Tanker freight rates have risen sharply over the last 18 months, helping to restore long-lost investor confidence in the tanker sector.
Mosvold said that average daily timecharter income for its first pair of VLCCs, Moscliff and Mosocean was $15,800 per day in the second quarter, up from $14,400 per day in the first quarter.
That renewed confidence can be seen in the performance of Mosvold shares this summer.

Shareholders who subscribed for new Mosvold shares at 8 Norwegian crowns each have already seen substantial gains. Mosvold shares opened on Tuesday at 13.80 crowns, before moving up to 13.90 crowns in early trading, an increase of over 73%. They touched a high of 14.50 on August 6.
Kristiansen said the company would have to digest its recent acquisitions before embarking on any further expansion.
"Over the past year, we have expanding significantly. First we took on a second VLCC last autumn, and now we have doubled that number to four," Kristiansen said.
"Obviously we have our hands full at the moment." -- Julian Bray, Reuters Shipping News +44 171 542 4087/4012. Fax 5017.
